analysis.one_liner: Blocked new Arctic oil and gas leasing until wildlife and spill-response safeguards were met.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote; it died in the House Natural Resources Committee after its May 2008 referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to bar the Interior Department from offering or approving any new oil and gas leases, seismic exploration, or development plans in the Beaufort and Chukchi Seas off Alaska until several conditions were met: the National Research Council reported on missing scientific information about the region's marine life, the polar bear received Endangered Species Act protection with designated critical habitat, the Interior Department completed an oil spill response gap analysis and demonstrated that 85 percent of any spill could be recovered within 30 days in any ice condition, and the Secretary determined that development could proceed without substantial harm to wildlife or Alaska Native subsistence. The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee on May 14, 2008 and never advanced further; the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 with no vote ever taken.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the bill would have protected the wildlife and marine ecosystems of the Beaufort and Chukchi Seas, including polar bears, bowhead whales, walrus, and seals, and the Alaska Native communities whose subsistence cultures depend on them. It also would have protected coastal communities from oil spill risk in ice-choked Arctic waters where the bill's findings said no effective means existed to recover spilled oil.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Alaska Native communities and Arctic wildlife

how_it_helps.text: The bill barred new leasing, seismic testing, and development approvals in the Beaufort and Chukchi Seas until the National Research Council identified missing science on the region's marine resources and Congress reviewed its report.
It required the polar bear to be listed as endangered or threatened under the Endangered Species Act with critical habitat designated before any new leasing could proceed.

It required an oil spill response gap analysis and a demonstrated ability to recover 85 percent of spilled oil within 30 days in any ice condition, addressing findings that no effective means existed to recover spilled oil in Arctic ice.

It required the Interior Secretary to determine that development could proceed without substantial adverse impacts to wildlife, habitat, or subsistence, and to implement all National Research Council recommendations.

analysis.who_pays: If passed, the bill would have delayed or prevented oil and gas companies from leasing and developing an estimated 73 million acres of Arctic offshore acreage planned under the Minerals Management Service's 2007-2012 leasing program, forgoing potential federal lease revenue and energy production.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies seeking Arctic leases

drawbacks.text: Delaying or blocking Arctic offshore leasing would forgo federal revenue from lease sales and potentially increase reliance on energy produced elsewhere, costs that an honest supporter would have to acknowledge.

The conditions were stringent — a demonstrated 85 percent oil recovery rate in any ice condition is a very high bar that the oil industry argued was technologically unattainable, meaning the bill could have functioned as a near-permanent moratorium rather than a pause pending better science.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill traded deferred energy development and federal lease revenue for stronger protection of a fragile Arctic ecosystem, Alaska Native subsistence cultures, and polar bear habitat already stressed by climate change. Its conditions were demanding enough that some would call it a de facto moratorium, but the bill's findings documented real gaps in spill-response capability and basic ecological science for the region.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Natural Resources Committee on May 14, 2008, and the committee never took it up; the 110th Congress ended with no vote ever scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Jay Inslee introduced the Polar Bear Seas Protection Act on May 14, 2008, with Rep. Maurice Hinchey as an original cosponsor, and it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources.
The bill attracted 26 Democratic cosponsors but no Republican support, and the House Natural Resources Committee never held a markup or scheduled the bill for floor action.
The 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, and the bill died in committee without receiving a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies interested in Arctic offshore leases were better off because the bill died; the Minerals Management Service proceeded with its planned leasing in the Beaufort and Chukchi Seas, including Lease Sale 193 in the Chukchi Sea, without the bill's required wildlife and spill-response conditions.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas companies seeking Arctic leases

for.name: Rep. Jay Inslee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 26 Democratic cosponsors.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a markup or floor action, letting it die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Alaska oil and gas interests
against.what_they_did: The bill's findings documented tribal opposition to offshore development but no recorded congressional action by industry; any industry lobbying against the bill is not in the record.

sides.party_line_note: All 26 cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill was introduced in a Democratic-majority House but never advanced out of committee, so no vote ever revealed the full partisan split.

industries.note: The bill would have blocked new leasing, seismic exploration, and development approvals across an estimated 73 million acres of planned Arctic offshore acreage until stringent wildlife and oil-spill-response conditions were met, directly preventing revenue and production the industry had planned under the federal 2007-2012 leasing program.

The bill's findings documented that tribal governments opposed offshore development because of threats to subsistence resources, public health, and cultural survival; the bill's leasing moratorium would have protected those interests.
